newsitem.title: USA: An update on Washington's various sex scandals ....
newsitem.headline: An update on Washington's various sex scandals ....

text.p: Once again, this Potomac River town, which only recently was obsessed with such mundane matters as balancing the budget, is awash in embarrassing tales of sexual shenanigans.
It is not as exciting as the time 20 years ago when powerful Congressman Wilbur Mills romped around the Tidal Basin with a stripper named Fannie Foxe.

But barely a day goes by without a screaming Page One headline about the latest development in the Paula Jones sexual harassment lawsuit against President Bill Clinton or adultery among the pillars of the U.S. military.

On the eve of the 53rd anniversary of the D-Day invasion, the Pentagon is reeling from revelations about marital cheating, which forced the discharge of B-52 pilot Kelly Flinn and several high-level resignations, and sexual harassment, which led to the transfer of the commander of the Aberdeen Proving Ground training school.

When the Gulf War was raging, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Colin Powell drew a defiant "line in the sand" over which Iraq must not cross. Today, Defence Secretary William Cohen has decided to draw a line and not let a mid-1980s adulterous affair by a four-star Air Force general, Joseph Ralston, disqualify him as the top candidate to become chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

In making his decision, Cohen said "the credibility to exercise moral leadership within the military does not come from notions of perfection" but rather from "the maturity, wisdom and courage to learn from our human errors."
How can Ralston get away with adultery but not Flinn, was the question from New York Democratic Representative Nita Lowey.

"It is very clear that the Pentagon is selectively enforcing its rules on sexual conduct," she said. "The Pentagon is employing a double standard. Some soldiers are getting a pat on the back -- some a slap on the wrist -- and some are getting booted from the Armed Services altogether."

But Washington pundit Stephen Hess said Cohen had probably found a good place to draw a line in the Ralston affair. "It happened a long time ago, he has a very distinguished record, and this is not the case of a flyer who has been in the Air Force for only a couple of years," he said.
Over at the White House, officials were cautious about embracing Ralston with open arms, saying he seemed a good pick but insisting Cohen had not yet formally recommended him.

The president has his own problems in the sexual harassment lawsuit by Jones, who contends Clinton asked her for oral sex in an Arkansas hotel room in 1991 when he was the state's governor and she a state employee.

Since the Supreme Court last week allowed her case to proceed, lawyers for both sides have engaged in a public crossfire. Clinton lawyer Robert Bennett threatened to bring up Jones' sexual past, but after a meeting with Clinton on Wednesday and an uproar from feminist groups he backed off.

Patricia Ireland, president of the National Organisation for Women, said she was sceptical about Bennett. "It is a classic defence to charges of sexual misconduct to try to discredit and intimidate women who bring such charges by portraying them as 'easy' women," Ireland said.

Underscoring the seaminess of the case, Jennifer Laszlo, a Democratic consultant who did some work for Clinton's re-election last year, summoned reporters last week to show them a videotape of a Jones lawyer, Gilbert Davis, making risque remarks to a female client in a hotel room.

Clinton, who profited mightily from the women's vote in his re-election, has been avoiding reporters since Bennett made his original threat. A news conference planned for next week has been cancelled and White House spokesman Mike McCurry has edgily referred all questions about it to Bennett.
